Subaru's In-House Electric Vehicle Outputs 510 HP, Uses Aisin Drive Units, Panasonic Battery Cells
16 photos
Photo: Subaru
Subaru has recently stuffed a 380-kilowatt electric drive system under a heavily modified Outback body shell. Underpinned by a completely new platform, this mule previews a future model that should give Scooby more control over its electric vehicles than the current Toyota-shared family allows.
As reported by Automotive News, the zero-emission mule is good for approximately 510 horsepower and under four seconds to 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour). Its wheelbase exceeds that of the donor vehicle, forcing a few interesting cuts around the wheel openings. That sort of awkwardness is customary of mules rather than pre-production prototypes.
The front motor apparently makes 150 kilowatts (201 horsepower) at full chatter, while its rear-mounted brother supplies 230 kilowatts (308 horsepower) in optimal conditions. More power and torque at the back gives the EV-centric platform a different starting point from a symmetrical pair of drive units, establishing a rear-biased setup. The control strategy, however, is a mystery for the time being.
As per engineering executive Takatomo Watamori, the Aisin-supplied motors were not selected for grunt alone. Instead, the Japanese automaker wants to preserve Subaru's trademark all-wheel-drive and safety priorities. Going independent with the development of this platform does not mean locking suppliers out, as demonstrated by the Aisin drive units.
Aisin, which is part of Toyota's larger group, remains the e-axle partner. Subaru announced this collab in March 2024, describing joint development and shared production of compact drive units. Panasonic, meanwhile, supplies battery expertise. Said relationships give Subaru architectural ownership, which is precisely the point of this project.
Photo: Subaru Its partnership with Toyota has already produced four models, namely the Solterra, Uncharted, Trailseeker, and Getaway. From the looks of it, the mule appears to fall somewhere between the dimensions of the Trailseeker and Getaway. The crash structure of the newcomer features new support members that curve over the front wheels to guide impact loads.
The front motor can rotate during a collision, thus absorbing energy. Subaru engineers aim to protect both occupants and the underfloor battery in the event of a crash. The company also targets a weight reduction of 100 kilograms (220 pounds) compared to the e-TNGA of Toyota, which is a modular design that also underpins the Lexus RZ and the Toyota C-HR+.
A lighter structure and better crash protection make for a great combination, and Subaru also worked its magic with the mule's battery pack. It contains nearly 4,000 cylindrical Panasonic cells, with the pack weighing 25 percent less than its e-TNGA batteries while targeting an energy density 20 percent above the industry average. Panasonic's involvement also dates back to March 2024.
Automotive News further learned about an integrated control unit covering powertrain, chassis, infotainment, and driver assistance duties, using a customized AMD SoC that supports over-the-air updates. Subaru wants to manufacture the units itself and share them across the lineup.
The final piece of the puzzle is Subaru confirming work with Infineon in March 2026 on a microcontroller for the integrated ECU, and this work is also expected to include AI integration into the EyeSight driver-assistance suite.
